title: Holly Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Holly wells have a 94-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, permit history and estimated drilling costs.
h1: Holly Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Holly means looking closely at the well record before you commit to a homesite. The permitted wells within five miles of Holly range from shallow plains wells to much deeper holes, and the records include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring uses.

Most reported wells produce substantial water, but the database is uneven: 546 permits are on record, while 316 are recorded as constructed, 344 report total depth, 80 report pump yield, and 10 report static water level. Use these figures to set expectations, then confirm the specific parcel with Colorado DWR records, a well contractor, and a proper site evaluation.

sections.heading: Holly well depths reflect shallow plains geology
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Holly is 94 feet. The middle half runs from 56 to 148 feet, which is the most useful range for an initial drilling estimate. Depths still vary widely: 53% of reported wells are under 100 feet, 34% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 12% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 1% exceed 600 feet.

The deepest well in the record is 815 feet. Local ground conditions are described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, but a particular lot can encounter different saturated zones, coarse material, or tighter rock. A driller should review nearby completion records rather than bid from the median alone. The 90th-percentile depth is 375 feet, so a contingency for a deeper hole matters when comparing bids.

sections.heading: Reported Holly yields are high, but the sample is limited
sections.html:
Among the 80 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 800.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 1462.5 gallons per minute, and 88% report at least 15 gallons per minute. The records show 12% in the 5-to-15-gallon-per-minute range, with 0% under 1 gallon per minute and 0% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures are not a guarantee for a new household well. The yield records are dominated by the local use mix, including 45% irrigation wells, compared with 14% domestic or household and 14% stock wells. Ask what test produced the reported yield, how long it ran, and whether the result applies to a domestic pump and storage system.

sections.heading: Holly water levels need parcel-specific checking
sections.html:
Only 10 permitted wells near Holly report a static water level, so the water-level dataset is too small to establish a dependable local trend. The reported median depth to static water is 145 feet, with the middle half from 74 to 212 feet.

That range is important when planning casing, pump placement, trenching, and electrical work. A shallow well depth does not automatically mean shallow water at every location, and a deeper water level can affect pump selection even when the drilled hole is not unusually deep. Ask for the well construction report and static water-level information for the actual property and nearby wells. The permit record includes 512 wells assigned to an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 11 in the Ogallala, and 6 in the Dakota Sandstone.

sections.heading: Holly permit history shows long-running well activity
sections.html:
Holly has a long permit history rather than a burst of only recent construction. The records show 7 permits from the 1950s, 28 from the 1960s, 60 from the 1970s, 23 from the 1980s, 50 from the 1990s, 76 from the 2000s, 71 from the 2010s, and 2 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in this dataset is 2021.

The most frequently listed drillers are Ark Valley Pump & Supply (Smith Jr., William), with 56 records; Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 49; and Ark Valley Pump & Supply (Smith, William David), with 43. Those names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a company is currently available. Verify licensing, insurance, references, and the proposed completion before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth Holly well pencils out at a specific range
sections.html:
For Holly's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 94-foot median depth, the drilled hole comes to about $3,300-$5,200. That is only the hole. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $9,300-$17,200.

A bid based on 94 feet may be reasonable for a typical shallow well, but it should not be treated as a fixed price. The record includes wells as deep as 815 feet, and the middle-half range extends to 148 feet. Request separate pricing for drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, electrical service, trenching, water testing, and any extra footage. Confirm what happens if the hole is dry or the yield is inadequate.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low-yield risk, and the homesite
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 historic mine feature. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped set. That does not establish the quality of a particular well. Test existing water before buying when possible, and plan baseline testing for a new well, especially if the property is near a mapped site or an older land use.

Low yield and dry holes remain site risks even though the reported pump-yield sample is strong. Check well spacing, casing and grout, pump condition, septic setbacks, and the location of the proposed drainfield before placing a house. A Colorado DWR permit controls the approved use. Household-use wells may be exempt wells, but an over-appropriated basin can require an augmentation plan for added use.

sections.heading: Compare nearby records before buying a Holly lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare permits and completion reports from nearby Holly wells and the surrounding areas of Hartman, Granada, Lamar, Sheridan Lake, and Brandon. Neighboring records can show the likely depth range, aquifer description, water level, and whether wells are used for household, stock, irrigation, or monitoring purposes.

For a purchase, make the well permit, recorded construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and septic approval part of your due diligence. For a new build, have a driller review access, the proposed well location, power, storage, trenching, and septic layout before excavation. In fractured or variable ground, do not assume the nearest well predicts your result. Get a written scope that explains depth allowances, testing, completion standards, and the response if the well does not meet the planned use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Holly, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Holly is 94 feet. The middle half runs from 56 to 148 feet, while the 90th percentile is 375 feet. Most are shallow, with 53% under 100 feet, but the deepest recorded well reaches 815 feet, so the nearby records should guide any site-specific estimate.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Holly, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 94-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,300-$5,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,300-$17,200. A deeper or difficult hole can cost more than the median-depth estimate.

faq.q: How much water do Holly wells produce?
faq.a: Among 80 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 800.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 1462.5 gallons per minute, and 88% report at least 15 gallons per minute. These results include many irrigation wells, so they should not be treated as a guarantee for a domestic well on a specific lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Holly, Colorado?
faq.a: The mapped area has 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 historic mine feature within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped facts do not determine an individual well's quality. Test the existing well before purchase and arrange baseline testing for a new well, particularly near a mapped environmental site.

faq.q: Do Holly wells have a falling water table?
faq.a: The available record cannot establish a reliable falling-water-table trend. Only 10 wells report static water level. Their median depth to water is 145 feet, with the middle half from 74 to 212 feet. Ask for the actual property's construction report and nearby static measurements instead of relying on a broad trend from this limited sample.
